references.text: Jesus immediately answers Peter's promise by predicting that Peter will deny him three times before the rooster crows ([ref:Luk 22:34|Luke 22:34]). Peter's confident declaration of readiness for prison and death is directly countered by Jesus' prophetic words.

The parallel passage in Matthew where Peter declares he will never fall away from Jesus, even if everyone else does, and that he is willing to die with him ([ref:Matt 26:33-35|Matthew 26:33-35]). Peter's overconfident self-assurance is a recurring theme in all the Gospel accounts.
Mark's parallel account where Peter insists that even if everyone else falls away, he will not, and that he is willing to die with Jesus ([ref:Mark 14:29-31|Mark 14:29-31]).

In John's Gospel, Peter declares he will give his life for Jesus, but Jesus responds by predicting his denial ([ref:Joh 13:37-38|John 13:37-38]). The same pattern of Peter's promise and Jesus' correction appears here.

The fulfillment of Jesus' prophecy: Peter follows Jesus to the high priest's courtyard, but instead of going to prison and dying with him, he denies Jesus three times ([ref:Luk 22:54-62|Luke 22:54-62]).

After the resurrection, Jesus restores Peter and predicts that Peter will one day actually follow Jesus in death ([ref:Joh 21:15-19|John 21:15-19]). What Peter promised in his overconfidence was ultimately fulfilled through God's grace.
After Pentecost, Peter's promise to go to prison for Jesus was fulfilled when the apostles were placed in public custody ([ref:Apg 5:17-18|Acts 5:17-18]).

Peter was actually thrown into prison by Herod ([ref:Apg 12:3-4|Acts 12:3-4]), showing that Peter's willingness to suffer for Christ eventually became reality—but only after he had been strengthened by the Holy Spirit.
"Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall" ([ref:Ordsp 16:18|Proverbs 16:18]). Peter's confident declaration illustrates the danger of relying too much on one's own strength.
